strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely theoretical question: when and how transfer learning helps in feature-learning rather than lazy infinite-width regimes.

The contribution is conceptually meaningful: it extends adaptive Bayesian kernel and DMFT-style analyses to a two-stage transfer setting with an elastic coupling between source and target hidden weights.
The theory produces interpretable mechanisms, especially the dependence of transfer benefit on source-target alignment, target sample size, elastic coupling strength, and feature-learning strength.

The synthetic experiments are well chosen for isolating phenomena: linear task alignment, low-to-high versus high-to-low polynomial transfer, and comparisons between finite-width simulations and the proposed infinite-width predictions.
The empirical curves generally show good qualitative, and sometimes close quantitative, agreement between the theory and large-width neural network simulations.

The related-work discussion is broad and positions the paper clearly relative to NTK/proportional-limit Bayesian transfer-learning theories, mean-field feature learning, and continual-learning dynamics.
weaknesses: The technical results are not fully rigorous. Key derivations rely on replica calculations, concentration assumptions, and a replica-symmetric ansatz, including informal justification such as choosing the solution that 'makes sense.' This is acceptable in some statistical-mechanics theory work but weakens the paper's formal claims.

The scope is narrow: the main theory is for two-layer networks, mostly square-loss regression or binary classification treated as regression, fixed finite datasets, and specific elastic coupling on hidden weights. The connection to practical fine-tuning of deep networks is therefore limited.

The real-data evidence is modest. CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST are reduced to small binary or simple grouped tasks, often grayscale/downsampled and trained with very wide shallow networks. This supports the theory but does not strongly validate claims about modern transfer learning.

There are few comparisons to alternative transfer mechanisms or baselines beyond random initialization and varying the elastic penalty. For example, standard fine-tuning, frozen features/linear probing, L2-SP-style penalties, or kernel baselines would help establish the practical and conceptual value of the proposed coupling.

Uncertainty and reproducibility details are limited. The paper reports large-width simulations but provides little information about random seeds, error bars, hyperparameter selection, numerical stability of saddle-point solvers, or code availability.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially statements that transfer learning is beneficial on real tasks 'at any feature learning strength' based on a small number of simplified binary experiments.

Presentation quality is generally good, but there are several rough edges and typos, and some notation is heavy enough that the main assumptions and limitations of each result are not always easy to identify.

strengths: The paper tackles an important question: when and why transfer learning helps in feature-learning neural networks, rather than only in lazy/kernel regimes.
It attempts to unify two complementary perspectives, Bayesian posterior analysis and gradient-flow/DMFT dynamics, for infinite-width two-layer networks under mean-field/µP scaling.

The synthetic experiments are reasonably aligned with the theory and illustrate interpretable phenomena such as dependence on source-target alignment, elastic coupling, feature-learning strength, and target sample size.
The paper includes several sanity checks where theory is compared against large-width simulations, and the qualitative agreement is a positive aspect.
weaknesses: The main theoretical results are not presented with sufficient rigor for a top-tier AI venue. The derivations rely heavily on replica/DMFT arguments, but assumptions, uniqueness/stability of saddle points, concentration statements, and regimes of validity are not clearly formalized.

The novelty appears incremental relative to adaptive neural Bayesian kernel and mean-field/DMFT prior work: the main new ingredient is an elastic coupling to pretrained weights, which is also closely related to prior Bayesian transfer/continual-learning formulations. The paper does not convincingly separate what is technically new from what follows mechanically from existing frameworks.

The evaluation is weak for the breadth of the claims. Real-data experiments are limited to small binary tasks with heavily simplified preprocessing, small target sample sizes, and two-layer networks, making the connection to modern transfer learning rather thin.

Important baselines and ablations are missing or underdeveloped: standard fine-tuning without elastic coupling, linear probing, frozen-feature baselines, source-only representations, random-feature baselines, sensitivity to weight decay/temperature/training time, and comparisons across seeds with error bars.

The paper reports mostly test loss curves and qualitative kernel visualizations, but gives little quantitative evidence of statistical reliability. Several plots appear cherry-picked, and class-pair choices on CIFAR/MNIST/Fashion-MNIST are not systematically explored.

The paper’s clarity and polish are below expectation. There are notation inconsistencies and apparent typos, such as switching between delta and eta, inconsistent initialization descriptions in the gradient-flow derivation, dimensionally confusing update equations, and informal phrases in the appendix.

The central claims are overstated. The work studies infinite-width two-layer models and small controlled tasks, but the introduction and discussion frame the contribution as a broad theory of transfer learning in modern neural networks.

Reproducibility is limited. Experimental details omit many implementation specifics, hyperparameter choices, seed information, dataset splits, and code availability, making it difficult to independently verify the empirical claims.

The limitations section is too brief and does not seriously address the gap between the analyzed setting and practical transfer learning in deep architectures, representation reuse, partial fine-tuning, large-scale pretrained models, or classification objectives.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and under-theorized problem: transfer learning when both source and target training can remain in a genuine feature-learning regime at infinite width, rather than reducing to lazy/kernel-only transfer.

The theoretical contribution is meaningful: the Bayesian adaptive-kernel formulation and the gradient-flow/DMFT formulation give complementary views of how source-task representations and target-task feature adaptation interact through an elastic coupling.

The paper gives useful qualitative predictions about when transfer helps or hurts, including dependence on source-target alignment, target sample size, feature-learning strength, and task complexity mismatch.
The synthetic experiments are well chosen for isolating mechanisms, especially the linear and polynomial teacher settings where task similarity and complexity can be controlled directly.
The finite-width simulations appear to track the proposed theory well across several settings, providing evidence that the infinite-width equations are not merely formal.
The appendices contain substantial derivational detail and additional experiments, including MNIST/Fashion-MNIST and a preliminary CNN extension.
weaknesses: The scope is still narrow relative to practical transfer learning: the main theory is for two-layer networks, mostly regression-style losses, and simplified supervised source/target tasks; the connection to modern deep fine-tuning remains largely conceptual.

The empirical evaluation is suggestive but not fully convincing for a top-tier AI venue. Real-data experiments are small-scale binary/class-subset tasks with grayscale/downsampled inputs, and the paper lacks comparisons to standard transfer/fine-tuning baselines beyond random initialization or varying the elastic coupling.

Several claims about real-task transfer are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, the CIFAR/MNIST-style results show trends in controlled small models, but do not establish broad predictive power for realistic transfer learning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: experimental details are sparse, code is not indicated, optimization procedures for solving the saddle-point/DMFT equations are not fully specified, and some hyperparameters/training protocols are only partially described.

There are presentation and consistency issues in the math. Some equations appear to contain notation or dimensional mistakes/typos, such as the gradient-flow statement in Result 2 and parts of the DMFT derivation, which makes independent verification harder.

The paper relies on replica/mean-field-style arguments without always making assumptions, saddle-point stability, or uniqueness conditions explicit. This is common in the area, but it weakens the level of rigor claimed by the theoretical results.

Limitations are acknowledged, but important ones are not deeply addressed: dataset averaging, depth, classification losses, finite-width corrections, and whether the elastic penalty is the right abstraction for practical transfer.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: when transfer learning helps in feature-learning regimes beyond lazy/kernel limits. The focus on infinite-width mean-field/µP networks is well motivated and relevant to current theory of representation learning.

The manuscript develops a coherent conceptual picture linking source data size, source-target alignment, feature-learning strength, and negative transfer. The linear toy models are especially useful because they expose interpretable mechanisms such as signal spikes, finite-sample noise spikes, crosstalk, and feature collapse under ultra-rich pretraining.

The paper makes a serious attempt to connect theory and phenomenology across several regimes: population and finite-source linear models, polynomial tasks, jointly rich transfer, and simple real-data image regression. The figures generally support the qualitative phase diagram claimed by the theory.

The work is well positioned relative to kernel regression, mean-field dynamics, Bayesian transfer, and continual-learning theory, and it appears to synthesize several strands into a unified transfer-learning framework.
weaknesses: The central theoretical results are not presented with enough rigor for a top-tier theory contribution. Several results rely on DMFT/path-integral saddle-point arguments, ansatzes, limiting-time manipulations, or unspecified constants, but the assumptions, convergence statements, and proof status are not always clear. For example, Result 3 leaves the key coefficients as implicit DMFT quantities and then derives conclusions mostly from special cases.

The empirical evaluation is mostly illustrative rather than convincing. The real-data experiments are limited to small two-class regression tasks with two-layer ReLU MLPs and very large width, rather than standard transfer-learning benchmarks or architectures. This makes it hard to assess whether the conclusions meaningfully generalize beyond the theoretical setup.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims a general theory of transfer learning in infinite-width feature-learning networks, but the tractable and quantitatively analyzed portions are mainly two-layer or linearized/simplified settings; deeper-network transfer is acknowledged as complex and largely deferred.

The comparison set is thin. Baselines are mostly training from scratch or lazy fine-tuning/kernel regression. There is little comparison against alternative transfer mechanisms, regularized fine-tuning, partial-layer freezing, representation reuse choices, or existing theoretical predictions where available.

Clarity and polish are uneven. Some result titles do not match the formal statements, notation is dense and occasionally inconsistent, and there are grammatical/typographical issues. The appendices contain many derivational steps but are hard to audit, which hurts reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Reproducibility details for experiments are insufficient from the main paper: hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing, exact training protocols, uncertainty over random seeds, and code availability are not clearly documented in the reviewed text. Error bars or variability estimates are largely absent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important theoretical question: when transfer learning helps or hurts in feature-learning neural networks, beyond lazy/kernel limits.

The manuscript attempts to connect several regimes in one framework, including infinite-width mean-field dynamics, fine-tuning with adaptive kernels, finite-source-data effects, ultra-rich pretraining, polynomial tasks, and small real-data experiments.

Some qualitative conclusions are interesting and plausible, especially the emphasis on source-target alignment, finite-sample noise causing negative transfer, and the possibility that overly rich source pretraining can collapse useful downstream features.
The paper includes nontrivial derivations and extensive appendices, suggesting significant technical effort.
weaknesses: The main theoretical results are often stated informally as 'Results' rather than precise theorems with clearly enumerated assumptions, convergence modes, and proof obligations. Several claims rely on heuristic DMFT, replica, or saddle-point arguments without enough rigor for the breadth of conclusions drawn.

The strongest general framing promises a theory of transfer learning in infinite-width multilayer feature-learning networks, but the analytically interpretable results mostly reduce to two-layer or linearized/toy settings. The gap between the ambitious claim and the actually controlled regimes is substantial.

Result 3 is particularly underdeveloped: key coefficients c1, c2, c3 are left as hard-to-compute constants, and the paper draws qualitative conclusions from special cases and ansatz choices rather than a complete predictive theory.

The empirical validation is weak for a top-tier AI venue. The real-data experiments are small binary regression tasks on CIFAR/Fashion-MNIST with two-layer MLPs, not realistic transfer learning settings, and they do not include modern architectures, standard transfer baselines, or robust comparisons.

The experiments mainly illustrate qualitative trends rather than convincingly validating the theory. There are limited ablations, little statistical reporting, unclear seed variability, and no strong evidence that the theory quantitatively predicts finite-width training beyond selected plots.

Important methodological details are underspecified, including optimization schedules, early stopping choices, hyperparameter selection, dataset preprocessing, and how theoretical predictions are numerically solved. This limits reproducibility.

The paper's positioning against closely related work is not fully convincing. It cites relevant transfer-learning and mean-field literature, but does not sharply distinguish which phenomena are genuinely new versus reinterpretations or extensions of prior adaptive-kernel and statistical-mechanics results.

Presentation quality is uneven. The manuscript contains grammatical issues, overloaded notation, occasional unclear definitions, and several places where conclusions are stated more strongly than the evidence supports. This makes the contribution harder to assess and reduces confidence in technical soundness.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: when feature-learning pretraining helps or hurts downstream transfer in infinite-width networks. The framing around source data size, source-target alignment, and feature-learning strength is useful and conceptually clarifying.

The theoretical contribution is substantial. The paper combines mean-field/DMFT dynamics for two-stage training with more tractable two-layer and linear specializations, yielding interpretable predictions such as positive transfer in data-rich source regimes, negative transfer from finite-source noise, and feature collapse under ultra-rich pretraining.

The work connects theory to phenomenology well. The synthetic linear and polynomial experiments illustrate the predicted regimes, and the finite-width ReLU simulations with DMFT curves provide evidence that the infinite-width theory is predictive beyond purely formal derivations.

The paper is well positioned relative to prior work on kernel transfer, mean-field feature learning, Bayesian transfer, and continual-learning dynamics. It clearly identifies what is new relative to fixed-kernel or source-infinite analyses.
The appendices are extensive and contain many derivational details, including deeper-network dynamics, proportional-regime calculations, simulation details, and a Bayesian extension.
weaknesses: Several central claims rely on highly idealized settings: two-layer networks, gradient flow, isotropic Gaussian inputs, regression losses, infinite width, and in some cases linear activations. The paper is careful about some limitations, but the title and framing can still read broader than what is technically established.

The finite-source-data result is less satisfying than the population result: the coefficients controlling signal, noise, and crosstalk are left as hard-to-compute DMFT constants, and the main empirical comparison uses an ansatz for their dependence on feature-learning strength. This weakens the quantitative predictive force of one of the paper's most interesting regimes.

The real-data evidence is suggestive but limited. CIFAR/MNIST-style binary regression tasks with very wide two-layer ReLU networks are far from modern transfer-learning practice, and there are no comparisons to stronger practical baselines, deeper architectures, classification losses, or standard pretrained representation protocols.

The general deep-network theory is presented as a complex framework but is not developed into concrete, testable predictions at the same level as the two-layer case. As a result, the strongest theoretical conclusions mostly come from simplified models.

Some notation and exposition are difficult to follow. There are many richness parameters, scaling conventions, and reused symbols, and several 'Result' statements mix formal claims with sketches or special cases. This may make independent verification hard for readers outside the narrow DMFT/statistical-physics community.

Reproducibility details appear incomplete for a top-tier empirical/theory paper: the manuscript describes simulations and Monte Carlo approximations, but the main text does not make clear whether code, hyperparameters, seeds, and numerical solvers will be released in a sufficiently usable form.
